stem: A fictional furniture shop in Lusaka buys a chair for US\$32 and sets its selling price by adding a mark-up of 45% to this cost.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the selling price of the chair.
parts.explanation: 32 × 1.45 = US\$46.40. Treating 45% as a margin on price gives US\$58.18.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 32 × 1.45 = US\$46.40. Treating 45% as a margin on price gives US\$58.18.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain one limitation of the shop's method of pricing.

points.description: Cost-plus pricing ignores what customers are willing to pay
Application: if rival shops sell similar chairs for less, the shop may lose sales at US\$46.40
The price is based on cost only, so it may be too low if customers would pay more

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cost-plus pricing ignores what customers are willing to pay. If rival shops sell similar chairs for less than US\$46.40, the shop may lose sales, and if customers would pay more the price is too low and profit is lost.

parts.explanation: One limitation, developed in context.

explanation: Price US\$46.40; cost-plus ignores demand and competition.
hints: Add the mark-up to the cost.

stem: A fictional hardware shop in Francistown sells 35 bags of cement a day. The supplier takes 4 days to deliver, and the shop keeps a buffer stock of 70 bags.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the re-order level.
parts.explanation: 35 × 4 + 70 = 140 + 70 = 210 bags. Leaving out the buffer gives 140.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 35 × 4 + 70 = 140 + 70 = 210 bags. Leaving out the buffer gives 140.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain one benefit to the shop of holding buffer inventory.

points.description: It protects against late deliveries, so the shop does not run out
Application: if the lorry is two days late, the shop can still sell 70 bags
Builders who need cement can still be served, so sales and loyalty are protected

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A buffer protects the shop against late deliveries. If the lorry is two days late, the shop can still sell the 70 bags in its buffer, so builders who need cement are served and sales and loyalty are protected.

parts.explanation: One benefit, developed in context.

explanation: Re-order level 210 bags; the buffer protects against late delivery.
hints: Re-order level = usage in the lead time + buffer.

stem:
Savanna Cycles is a fictional bicycle assembler in Johannesburg. In Year 2 it cut its price slightly and increased promotion, and sales rose. The painting of the frames is done in the company's own paint shop, which has fixed costs of US\$28,000 a year, with a variable cost of US\$5.10 a bicycle. A specialist painting company has offered to paint all frames at US\$6.50 a bicycle. A large retailer has also asked to buy 2,400 extra bicycles in Year 3 at US\$152 each; the variable cost of materials and assembly is US\$112 a bicycle, and the other costs would not change. Some managers fear that the retailer's low price would make other retailers ask for the same.

|  | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Bicycles assembled and sold | 9,600 | 10,800 |
| Maximum capacity (bicycles a year) | 14,400 | 14,400 |
| Employees | 48 | 48 |
| Labour cost (US\$) | 230,400 | 226,800 |
| Selling price per bicycle (US\$) | 180 | 175 |
| Promotion spending (US\$) | 19,200 | 27,000 |

Unit labour cost = labour cost ÷ output.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Output divided by the number of employees is {{blank:a}}, while actual output as a percentage of maximum output is {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: Output per employee is labour productivity; actual output over maximum output is capacity utilisation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: For Year 2, calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the capacity utilisation, to one decimal place;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the labour productivity, in bicycles per employee.
parts.explanation: 10,800 ÷ 48 = 225 bicycles per employee.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the unit labour cost in Year 2;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the percentage change in unit labour cost between Year 1 (US\$24.00) and Year 2, to one decimal place (give a fall as a negative number).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain two effects on Savanna Cycles of operating at 75% capacity utilisation.

points.description: Fixed costs are spread over fewer bicycles than the plant could make, so unit costs are higher
Application: the paint shop's fixed costs of US\$28,000 are shared by 10,800 bicycles instead of 14,400
Spare capacity of 3,600 bicycles allows the company to accept extra orders without new investment
Application: the retailer's request for 2,400 bicycles can be met within the spare capacity
Idle workers or machines may reduce morale and the efficiency of the business

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At 75% capacity the fixed costs, such as the paint shop's US\$28,000, are spread over 10,800 bicycles rather than 14,400, so the cost of each bicycle is higher. On the other hand, there is spare capacity of 3,600 bicycles, so the company can accept the retailer's request for 2,400 bicycles without new investment. Idle workers or machines may also reduce morale and efficiency.

parts.explanation: Two effects, one adverse and one favourable, developed in context.
hints: Think about costs per unit and about the retailer's order.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Analyse the advantages and disadvantages to Savanna Cycles of outsourcing the painting of frames.

points.description: In-house painting costs 5.10 × 10,800 + 28,000 = US\$83,080 a year
Outsourcing costs 6.50 × 10,800 = US\$70,200, a saving of US\$12,880 a year
The saving arises because the paint shop's fixed costs of US\$28,000 are removed
The specialist may provide better quality painting and allow Savanna to focus on assembly
Savanna has less control over quality and delivery times of painted frames
The company becomes dependent on one supplier, which could raise its price later
Painters may lose their jobs, damaging morale among remaining staff

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Painting in-house costs 5.10 × 10,800 + 28,000 = US\$83,080 a year, while outsourcing costs 6.50 × 10,800 = US\$70,200, a saving of US\$12,880, because the fixed costs of US\$28,000 are removed. The specialist may also provide a better finish and let Savanna focus on assembly. However, the company would have less control over the quality and delivery of frames, would depend on one supplier that could raise its price later, and the painters could lose their jobs, which would damage morale among the remaining staff.

parts.explanation: Cost comparison plus control, dependence and morale.
hints: Compare the in-house cost with the outsourced cost first.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Savanna Cycles should accept the retailer's request to buy 2,400 extra bicycles at US\$152 each.

points.description: The contribution on each bicycle is 152 − 112 = US\$40
The extra contribution is 2,400 × 40 = US\$96,000, because other costs would not change
Spare capacity is 3,600 bicycles, enough for the extra 2,400
Utilisation would rise from 75.0% to 91.7%, reducing fixed cost per bicycle
The price of US\$152 is below the normal price of US\$175, and other retailers may ask for the same
Higher utilisation leaves less room for breakdowns or late deliveries
Judgement with a reason, for example: accept, because the contribution is large
Condition or time-frame, for example: if the order can be kept separate from other retailers

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation using the figures, with a justified judgement and a condition
Reasons for and against using some figures
General points with little use of the case

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The contribution on each bicycle is 152 − 112 = US\$40, so the 2,400 extra bicycles add US\$96,000, because other costs would not change. Spare capacity is 3,600, so the order can be met, and utilisation would rise from 75.0% to 91.7%, which spreads fixed costs over more bicycles. On the other hand, the price of US\$152 is below the normal US\$175, so other retailers may ask for the same, and higher utilisation leaves less room for breakdowns. Savanna should accept, because the contribution is large, as long as the order is clearly separate from its normal sales; if other retailers demand the same price, the gain could be lost.

parts.explanation: Contribution of US\$96,000 weighed against the risk of price cuts to other retailers.
hints: Calculate the contribution on the extra order first.

explanation: Utilisation 75.0%, productivity 225, unit labour cost down 12.5%; outsourcing saves US\$12,880; the order adds US\$96,000 contribution.

stem: Essay. A fictional clothing retailer in Harare has two shops and promotes itself through posters and radio. The owner is considering moving most of the promotion to social media and the company's own website.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Analyse two benefits to the retailer of using digital marketing. [8 marks]

points.description: Social media can target particular groups, such as young shoppers
Application: adverts can be shown to people interested in fashion in Harare
Targeting wastes less money on people unlikely to buy
Results can be measured, such as clicks, visits and orders
Application: the owner can see which posts bring customers into the shops or onto the website
The owner can then spend more on what works and less on what does not
A website lets customers see and order clothes at any time
Application: customers outside Harare could buy, widening the market

levels.descriptor: Two benefits analysed with developed chains and application to the retailer
Two benefits explained with some application
Benefits stated with little development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Social media can target particular groups such as young shoppers interested in fashion, so less money is wasted on people who are unlikely to buy. The results can also be measured, for example by the clicks and orders each post produces, so the owner can spend more on what works and less on what does not. A website would also let customers outside Harare see and order clothes at any time, which widens the market.

parts.explanation: Two benefits with chains of analysis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the retailer should rely mainly on digital promotion rather than posters and radio. [12 marks]

points.description: Digital promotion is cheaper per customer reached and can be targeted
Results can be measured, helping the owner to improve
Customers outside Harare can be reached, widening the market
Posters and radio reach customers who do not use the internet or have little data
Application: in-shop customers in Harare may respond more to local radio and posters
Radio and posters build local awareness and trust in the brand
Digital marketing needs skills, time and constant attention, and complaints are public
Delivery, security and trust matter if the website sells online
A mix of methods spreads risk and reaches different customer groups
The best balance depends on the retailer's customers and budget
Judgement with a reason, for example: digital for young customers and radio for others
Condition or time-frame, for example: test for six months and compare sales by method

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation of both approaches using the retailer's customers, with a justified judgement and a condition
Reasons for and against with some application and a judgement
General points on promotion with little application

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Digital promotion is cheaper per customer reached and can be targeted at particular groups, and the results can be measured, so the owner can see what works. A website could also reach customers outside Harare. However, posters and radio reach customers who do not use the internet or have limited data, and they build local trust in the brand. Digital marketing also needs skills and constant attention, and public complaints can harm a small brand. The owner should not rely mainly on digital promotion until she knows how her customers find her shops. A sensible choice is digital promotion for younger customers and radio for others, tested for six months and judged by the sales each method produces.

parts.explanation: Both approaches weighed with a judgement and a condition.

explanation: Digital marketing offers targeting and measurement; the choice depends on the retailer's customers and on testing the results.
hints: Link the benefits to the retailer's shops and customers.

stem: Essay. Marula Ceramics is a fictional maker of plates and bowls in Gaborone. About 6% of its products are found faulty at final inspection, and last year customers returned a further 3%. The owner is considering introducing total quality management (TQM), which would cost money for training and for meetings of quality circles, and would involve all 120 employees. Some supervisors say that inspection should simply be made stricter.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Analyse two benefits to Marula Ceramics of introducing TQM. [8 marks]

points.description: TQM makes every employee responsible for quality at every stage
Application: faults would be found at the stage where they arise, not at final inspection
Fewer faulty plates are made, so waste and rework fall
Application: the 6% of products found faulty is a cost that TQM aims to reduce
Quality circles use workers' knowledge to solve problems
Involvement raises motivation and care
Fewer returns (now 3%) protect the company's reputation
Application: better reputation helps to win repeat orders and allows higher prices

levels.descriptor: Two benefits analysed with developed chains and application to Marula Ceramics
Two benefits explained with some application
Benefits stated with little development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: TQM makes every employee responsible for quality, so faults are found at the stage where they arise rather than at final inspection. Fewer faulty plates are made, so waste and rework fall, and this reduces the cost of the 6% of products that are now found faulty. Quality circles use the workers' knowledge to solve problems and raise motivation. Fewer returns, now 3%, would also protect the company's reputation and help it to win repeat orders and charge higher prices.

parts.explanation: Two benefits with chains of analysis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether introducing TQM is the best way for Marula Ceramics to improve quality. [12 marks]

points.description: TQM tackles the causes of faults rather than only finding them
Stricter inspection would find more faulty plates before they are sold, but would not stop them being made
Application: 6% faulty at inspection is wasted material and labour even if they are never sold
Inspection adds the cost of inspectors and cannot find every fault, as returns of 3% show
TQM needs training, time and meetings, which cost money and output
Success depends on the commitment of all 120 employees and managers
Some supervisors resist, so change may be slow
Benefits come over time, not at once
Benchmarking against the best firm could set targets
A combination of TQM with some inspection checks results
Judgement with a reason, for example: TQM is better in the long run for the number of faults
Condition or time-frame, for example: if staff are committed and results are measured over a year

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation using the company's data, with a justified judgement and a condition
Reasons for and against with some application and a judgement
General points on quality with little application

answerSpec.modelAnswer: TQM tackles the causes of faults, so fewer faulty plates are made, whereas stricter inspection only finds more of them after the material and labour have been wasted: 6% of production is already faulty at inspection, and the 3% returned shows that inspection misses some faults. Against TQM, training and quality circles cost money and time, the benefits come slowly, and success depends on the commitment of all 120 employees, while some supervisors are already resistant. A combination, with TQM supported by some inspection and a benchmark against the best firm, is more likely to work than either alone. TQM is the better way to improve quality in the long run, provided that staff are committed and results are measured over a year.

parts.explanation: TQM compared with stricter inspection, with a judgement and a condition.

explanation: TQM prevents faults but needs commitment and time; inspection finds faults only after they are made.
hints: Compare preventing faults with finding them.

stem:
Botswana Beverages is a fictional bottler that has expanded its output in two stages. The table shows total costs at three output levels.

| Output (units) | Total cost (US\$) |
| --- | ---: |
| 25,000 | 175,000 |
| 60,000 | 330,000 |
| 120,000 | 744,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage change in average cost per unit when output rises from 25,000 to 60,000 units, to one decimal place (give a fall as a negative number).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse why average cost per unit rose when output increased from 60,000 to 120,000 units.

points.description: Average cost rose from US\$5.50 to US\$6.20 per unit
Diseconomies of scale: the company has become too large to manage efficiently
Communication is slower and decisions take longer
Workers feel less involved and motivation and productivity fall
Total cost more than doubled while output only doubled, so cost per unit rose

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Average cost rose from US\$5.50 to US\$6.20 a unit. This suggests diseconomies of scale: the company has become too large to manage efficiently, so communication and decisions are slower. Workers may feel less involved, so motivation and productivity fall. Total cost rose from US\$330,000 to US\$744,000, more than doubling, while output only doubled, so the cost of each unit rose.

parts.explanation: Diseconomies of scale explained, with the figures.
hints: Compare how fast total cost and output have risen.

explanation: Average cost falls 21.4% to 60,000 units, then rises to US\$6.20 at 120,000: economies, then diseconomies of scale.

stem: Marula Ceramics is a fictional maker of plates in Gaborone that produces 40,000 plates a year. At present 5% of plates are defective, each costing US\$4.50 in scrap and lost materials. The company expects total quality management (TQM) to cut the defect rate to 2%.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the yearly saving from the expected fall in the defect rate.
parts.explanation: Defects now = 5% × 40,000 = 2,000, costing US\$9,000. After TQM = 2% × 40,000 = 800, costing US\$3,600. Saving = US\$5,400.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain one way in which TQM could reduce the defect rate.

points.description: TQM makes every worker responsible for checking quality at their own stage
Application: a worker who finds a fault in a plate stops it from moving on, so faults are found early
Training and quality circles help workers to find the causes of faults and remove them
Fewer faults are made at the source, so waste and the 5% defect rate fall

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: TQM makes every worker responsible for checking quality at their own stage, so a worker who finds a fault in a plate stops it from moving on and faults are found early. Training and quality circles help workers to find the causes of faults and remove them, so fewer faults are made and the defect rate falls.

parts.explanation: One way, developed with a chain to the defect rate.
hints: Think about who checks quality under TQM.

explanation: Defects cost US\$9,000 now and US\$3,600 after TQM, a saving of US\$5,400; TQM reduces faults at source.
hints: Find the cost of defects before and after TQM.

stem:
Baobab Packaging is a fictional maker of cartons based in Johannesburg. Its main customers are within 30 km of its factory. The owner is considering moving to a town 400 km away, where rent and labour are cheaper but transport costs to customers would be higher. The move would cost US\$135,000. About 40% of the experienced staff say they would not move. The factory building is old and the lease will end in two years.

| Yearly cost (US\$) | Present site (Johannesburg) | Proposed site |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Rent | 96,000 | 60,000 |
| Labour | 310,000 | 270,000 |
| Transport | 51,000 | 72,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the total yearly cost of the proposed site;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the yearly saving from moving.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse one qualitative factor that Baobab Packaging should consider before moving.

points.description: Loss of experienced staff: about 40% would not move
Application: new staff must be recruited and trained, so output and quality may fall at first
Distance from customers: 400 km from the present customers
Application: delivery would take longer and cost more, which could lose orders to local rivals

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: About 40% of the experienced staff would not move, so new staff must be recruited and trained, and output and quality may fall at first. The new site is also 400 km from the present customers, so delivery would take longer and could lose orders to local rivals.

parts.explanation: One factor, analysed with the case.
hints: Use the staff and customer information in the case.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Baobab Packaging should move to the proposed site.

points.description: Yearly cost falls by US\$55,000 (from US\$457,000 to US\$402,000), a saving of 12.0%
The move costs US\$135,000, which the saving repays in about 2.5 years (135,000 ÷ 55,000)
The lease on the present building ends in two years, so a decision is needed anyway
Higher transport costs of US\$72,000 could rise further if fuel costs rise or customers move
The loss of 40% of the experienced staff may reduce quality and productivity
Customers 400 km away may switch to local rivals, which the cost figures do not show
Judgement with a reason, for example: move, since the saving repays the cost quickly
Condition or time-frame, for example: if key customers will stay and enough staff can be recruited

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation using the cost figures and qualitative factors, with a justified judgement and a condition
Reasons for and against with some use of figures
General points on relocation with little use of the case

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The proposed site would cut yearly costs by US\$55,000, from US\$457,000 to US\$402,000, and the US\$135,000 cost of moving would be repaid in about 2.5 years. The present lease ends in two years, so the company must decide anyway. Against this, transport costs rise to US\$72,000 and could rise further, 40% of the experienced staff would not move, and customers 400 km away may switch to local rivals, which the figures do not show. The company should move only if its main customers will stay with it and enough skilled workers can be recruited; otherwise it should look for a cheaper site nearer Johannesburg.

parts.explanation: Saving of US\$55,000 and payback of 2.5 years against the loss of staff and customers.
hints: Use the payback period and the risks to customers and staff.

explanation: The proposed site saves US\$55,000 a year and repays the move in 2.5 years, but staff and customers are at risk.
hints: Add rent, labour and transport for each site.

stem: Kgosi Garments is a fictional clothing company in Gaborone. Three years ago it offshored its sewing to a country with lower wages. The cost of making a garment there is now US\$6.10, plus US\$0.90 for shipping and US\$0.60 import duty, a total of US\$7.60. Making the garment in Gaborone would cost US\$7.40. About 6% of the garments made overseas are defective, against 2% if made at home, and each defective garment costs US\$8 to replace. Delivery now takes eight weeks, and retailers have started to complain about late deliveries. The company's former employees in Gaborone have mostly found other work, so restarting production would need new training. Evaluate whether Kgosi Garments should reshore its sewing to Gaborone.

points.description: Production abroad now costs US\$7.60 a garment including shipping and duty, close to US\$7.40 at home
Allowing for defects (6% × US\$8 = US\$0.48), the overseas cost is US\$8.08
Defects at home (2% × US\$8 = US\$0.16) give a cost of US\$7.56, so home production is cheaper by about US\$0.52
Delivery of eight weeks is slow and has led to complaints from retailers
Reshoring would shorten the supply chain and give more control over quality
Quality would improve, with defects falling from 6% to 2%
The workers in Gaborone have gone, so new staff would need training and output may fall at first
Setting up production again requires investment and time
The cost advantage of overseas wages has gone, but wages and shipping costs may change again
Reshoring supports local jobs and may be seen favourably by customers
A partial approach (some production at home for quick-turn orders) reduces the risk
Judgement with a reason and a condition, for example reshore if the savings repay the set-up cost within a few years

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation using the cost and defect figures and the delivery and training issues; considers a partial approach; a justified judgement with a condition
Analyses costs and problems with application; some evaluation; judgement supported
Explains benefits or problems with some application; limited judgement
Describes reshoring with little application

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Production overseas now costs US\$7.60 a garment including shipping and duty, close to the US\$7.40 it would cost at home. When defects are included, 6% × US\$8 = US\$0.48 raises the overseas cost to US\$8.08, while 2% defects at home add US\$0.16, giving US\$7.56, so home production is cheaper by about US\$0.52 a garment. Delivery of eight weeks has also led to complaints, and a shorter supply chain would give more control over quality. Against reshoring, the former employees have mostly left, so new staff would have to be trained and output may fall at first, and restarting production requires investment. Wages and shipping costs may also change again. Overall, reshoring appears justified: it is cheaper on the figures and improves delivery and quality. A sensible approach is to reshore in stages, keeping some overseas production for large orders, and to go ahead fully only if the savings repay the set-up cost within about three years.

explanation: Overseas cost with defects US\$8.08 against US\$7.56 at home; delivery and quality favour reshoring, while retraining and set-up cost are risks.
hints: Include defects in the cost comparison.
